HCBCOGN312.topics: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? candidateDecisions.label: English linguistics, language in society and cognition

analysis: The closest option combines genre and close reading, world literature, life writing and literary theory with stylistics, psycholinguistics, rhetoric and contextual work in film and the American Century. Rhetoric in Action moves to the final spring after the introductory course and complements the documentary, historical and creative projects. The literature and media option adds film history, media archaeology, empire, Indigenous histories, gender and museum and art-history methods. Heritage and ancient democracy contribute contextual interpretation and contested citizenship, rather than English literary history. The language option builds from Brain & Behavior and rhetoric into psycholinguistics, language and style, philosophy of mind and later work on higher cognition, persuasion and research synthesis. Conflict and social theory are contextual contributions to public discourse and identity. Description-only Psycholinguistics gives direct acquisition and language-processing evidence, Perspectives on Literary Meaning supports critical theory, Writing Art’s Histories supports historiography and Communicating the Climate Crisis contributes analysis of public argument. The three alternatives exceed the pairwise course-difference floor. The alignment preserves the modern and medieval English literary sequences, conversation analysis, sociolinguistics, teaching English and the final project as distinct requirements. The poetry lab and psychology meta-analysis remain complementary courses, without claims of interactional linguistics or subject-specific thesis equivalence. The 15 EC optional UCR research element is comparison-only.
